extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political theory, historians, policymakers interested in democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and evaluative principles about associations, suffrage, elections, and public officers in democratic societies as presented in a chapter of a classical political treatise. Useful for assessing how democratic institutional features affect liberty, governance, and public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of association as guarantee against majority tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of association ... has become a necessary guarantee against the tyranny of the majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associations are especially needed in democracies because once a party becomes preponderant "all public authority passes under its control"; minorities form associations to oppose the moral authority of the majority and to establish themselves upon a basis. The text treats the right of association as nearly inalienable and asserts that no legislator can attack it without impairing the foundations of society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associations should be peaceable and legal (American model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political associations in the United States are therefore peaceable in their intentions, and strictly legal in the means which they employ; and they assert with perfect truth that they only aim at success by lawful expedients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the U.S. associations primarily aim to show numerical strength and to persuade the majority, not to prepare for immediate action. They borrow forms from civil administration and preserve individual independence within the association; contrast with European associations that are organized for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: European associations tend toward militarized, action-oriented form
rubrics_metrics.description: In Europe a society is often "an army" where the idea of impending action prevails; associations centralize direction, intrust power to a few leaders, and impose passive obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This organizational model involves watchwords, passive obedience, and abjuring personal judgment — producing tyrannical internal control and diminishing the moral force of the association. The text treats this as an anti-pattern relative to deliberative, legal association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of unrestrained liberty of association
rubrics_metrics.description: If the liberty of association does not throw the nation into anarchy, it perpetually augments the chances of that calamity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberty of association can be perverted or carried to excess; the author warns it may become "an element of destruction." The danger is more acute in inexperienced democracies where association is seen primarily as a right to attack government rather than to persuade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free associations prevent secret conspiracies
rubrics_metrics.description: In countries where associations are free, secret societies are unknown. In America there are numerous factions, but no conspiracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of open, legal associations channels dissent into visible, non-conspiratorial forms of politics, which is presented as a stabilizing advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal suffrage is widespread but not a guarantee of wise choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal Suffrage ... is by no means a guarantee of the wisdom of the popular choice, and that, whatever its advantages may be, this is not one of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although universal suffrage allows broad participation, the text argues it does not ensure that the most able men rise to head public affairs because the mass lacks time, means, and the inclination for deep evaluation of candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic propensity to exclude distinguished men from office
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States the most able men are very rarely placed at the head of affairs; the race of American statesmen has dwindled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes include limits on popular education/time, envy and resentment fostered by democratic passion for equality, and the fact that talented individuals often seclude themselves from politics because independence is hard to keep and advancement tends to degrade them politically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions that correct democratic selection failures
rubrics_metrics.description: When a State is threatened by serious dangers, the people frequently succeeds in selecting the citizens who are the most able to save it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraordinary circumstances (war, crisis) can bring great characters to the fore; also local variations in education, manners, and stability (e.g., New England vs. South-west) influence the quality of popular choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect election (election by an elected body) refines representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate is elected by elected bodies ... this transmission of the popular authority through an assembly of chosen men operates an important change in it, by refining its discretion and improving the forms which it adopts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect election tends to produce assemblies that represent "elevated thoughts" rather than petty passions; the contrast between the House (directly elected, more vulgar) and the Senate (indirectly elected, more illustrious) is used to argue for occasional use of indirect election to mitigate democratic excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of elections: trade-off between revolution and legal mutability
rubrics_metrics.description: When elections are rare, they expose the State to a violent crisis—When they are frequent, they keep up a degree of feverish excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent elections reduce the stakes of any single contest (less risk of revolution) but produce legislative instability and "mutability of the laws." The Americans chose frequent elections, accepting instability as preferable to violent crises; Hamilton and Jefferson noted dangers of excessive law-making and mutability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple exterior and accessibility of public officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Public officers in the United States are commingled with the crowd of citizens; they have neither palaces, nor guards, nor ceremonial costumes ... A public officer in the United States is uniformly civil, accessible to all the world, attentive to all requests, and obliging in his replies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity of external trappings is linked to democratic principles and is not held to reduce respect for office. The author argues that emblems of authority are unnecessary and sometimes harmful to dignity if they encourage abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remuneration of public officers as democratic principle
rubrics_metrics.description: All public services, of whatsoever nature they may be, are paid; so that every one has not merely the right, but also the means of performing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment of public officers prevents public service from becoming the preserve of the wealthy and preserves democratic access. The substitution of paid for unpaid functionaries (or vice versa) signals a shift toward monarchical or despotic institutions; remuneration thus has constitutional significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a professional political career under democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: In nations in which the principle of election extends to every place in the State no political career can, properly speaking, be said to exist. Men are promoted as if by chance to the rank which they enjoy, and they are by no means sure of retaining it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because offices are not secure career paths and often remunerated only modestly, many talented individuals avoid public life; public functions offer few lures to ambition in tranquil times, which affects the quality of officeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater arbitrary power of magistrates under democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: In two different kinds of government the magistrates exercise a considerable degree of arbitrary power; namely, under the absolute government of a single individual, and under that of a democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under democracy the majority tends to leave officers considerable latitude rather than restrain them by invariable rules, producing significant arbitrary discretion by magistrates. The text warns this is analogous to arbitrarness in despotic states, though arising from different causes.
